question: What low-rank structures recur in large-model weights, updates, gradients, and activations, and which optimization arguments explain their emergence or justify exploiting them?

key_findings.claim: The review distinguishes four locations of low rank—weights, adapters/updates, gradients, and activations—and warns that evidence for one does not automatically justify assumptions about another.
key_findings.evidence: Its organizing taxonomy separates explicit matrix factorization from low-dimensional training trajectories and representation bottlenecks, then maps training, PEFT, compression, dropout, and masked learning methods onto those objects.

key_findings.claim: One theoretical lens is finite-time gradient dynamics: under structured initialization, deep matrix factorization and overparameterized adapters can keep updates inside invariant low-dimensional subspaces.
key_findings.evidence: The survey develops singular-value dynamics and invariant-subspace results, using them to interpret LoRA-like factors, deeper low-rank adapters, GaLore, and periodically refreshed projected-gradient methods.

key_findings.claim: A second lens is implicit bias at convergence: factorized homogeneous linear models can select solutions characterized by Schatten-type or nuclear-norm preferences even without an explicit rank penalty.
key_findings.evidence: The review relates depth, balance, and loss choice to induced matrix regularization, while noting that extensions from deep linear products to nonlinear modern networks are incomplete.

key_findings.claim: Observed spectral decay motivates compression but is heterogeneous across layers and objectives, so a fixed global rank is a weak default.
key_findings.evidence: Transformer and vision examples show stronger low-rank structure in some deeper layers than in early layers, and dropout/masked objectives reshape activation spectra. The review repeatedly motivates adaptive layerwise rank and calls for theory that predicts useful rank from data and training.

method.core_idea: Synthesize low-rank large-model research by the mathematical object being compressed and by whether rank is imposed, dynamically preserved, or selected implicitly.
method.mechanism: The tutorial derives core matrix-factorization and gradient-flow results, illustrates them with singular-value trajectories, then surveys low-rank adapters, projected optimizers, low-rank training, hypernetwork/PINN variants, dropout, and masked learning through a shared spectral vocabulary.
assumptions: Deep-linear and matrix-factorization results provide informative mechanisms for nonlinear large networks.
Small singular values can often be removed without destroying task-relevant information.
Empirical spectra measured at selected layers/checkpoints are representative of broader model behavior.
Low-dimensional optimization trajectories remain stable when optimizers, normalization, and data distributions change.

techniques.role: Diagnoses numerical rank in weights, activations, and updates.
Provides a tractable model of rank growth and implicit regularization.
Explains when finite-time updates remain compressible.
Characterizes low-rank preference of factorized optimization at convergence.

evaluations.setting: Deep matrix factorization and deep low-rank adaptation examples.
evaluations.result: Illustrations show structured low-dimensional evolution consistent with the reviewed invariant-subspace theory.

evaluations.setting: BERT adaptation on STS-B and related PEFT illustrations.
evaluations.metric: Layerwise spectra of accumulated updates and adapter factors.
evaluations.result: Updates concentrate in relatively few directions, supporting low-rank adaptation while exposing imbalance from asymmetric factor initialization.
evaluations.baseline: Full fine-tuning and standard shallow LoRA parameterization.

evaluations.setting: Vision-transformer projections and deep-network activation spectra under dropout or masked training.
evaluations.result: Low-rank structure is pronounced in selected deeper layers and varies materially with training objective, rather than appearing uniformly.
evaluations.baseline: Early layers and corresponding models without the compared masking/dropout setting.

limitations: This is a selective tutorial and synthesis rather than a systematic review with a reproducible search protocol.
Many formal results hold for deep linear or idealized factorized models, not realistic transformers.
Singular-value decay alone does not prove that truncated directions are irrelevant to rare behaviors or transfer.
The field changes quickly, so method and scaling comparisons are necessarily time-bounded.
failure_modes: A rank chosen on one task or layer can bottleneck another task or erase low-frequency but important directions.
Projected optimizers can miss newly emerging gradient directions between subspace refreshes.
Factor imbalance can make nominally low-rank adaptation optimize slowly or unstably.
Apparent numerical rank can be an artifact of threshold, normalization, or finite precision.
reusable_insights: Always specify whether a low-rank claim concerns weights, updates, gradients, or activations.
Separate finite-time trajectory confinement from convergence-time implicit bias; they answer different questions.
Rank should usually be allocated layerwise and adaptively rather than fixed globally.
open_questions: Which data and architecture statistics predict the minimum safe layerwise rank before expensive training?
When do low-rank subspaces rotate fast enough that projected optimization loses its memory advantage?
Can nonlinear-network theory connect spectral compression to downstream robustness and rare-capability retention?

competitive_landscape.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Introduces the dominant low-rank update parameterization for parameter-efficient adaptation.
competitive_landscape.difference: LoRA is one method and empirical hypothesis; this paper synthesizes it with low-rank training dynamics, implicit bias, gradients, and representations.

competitive_landscape.title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
competitive_landscape.relationship: Combines low-rank adapters with quantized frozen base weights for memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning.
competitive_landscape.difference: QLoRA is an engineering recipe for adaptation memory; the review examines why low-rank parameter and gradient structure may arise and where that assumption can fail.

competitive_landscape.title: GaLore: Memory-Efficient LLM Training by Gradient Low-Rank Projection
competitive_landscape.relationship: Exploits low-rank gradient subspaces to reduce optimizer-state memory during full-parameter training.
competitive_landscape.difference: GaLore operationalizes one surveyed object—the gradient—whereas the review compares that mechanism with low-rank weights, updates, and activations and discusses invariant-subspace theory.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The survey offers a unified optimization-centered account of low-rank structures across training and adaptation of large models.
novelty_assessment.evidence: It organizes disparate methods by object and time scale, develops two complementary theoretical lenses, and connects them to representative spectra and algorithms.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Its value is conceptual integration and tutorial derivation rather than a new low-rank algorithm; the taxonomy usefully prevents category errors common in the literature.

reviewer_notes: Read the complete 37-page tutorial including theoretical and algorithm appendices. The comparison panel uses primary papers for three central method families, checked on 2026-08-23.
